chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 331 to 340, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade of the wife's lament (தலைவி இரங்கு பத்து): every poem opens on அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the wife, her man gone across the waste for wealth, measures his leaving against the beasts and birds that should have stopped him, against stone, against the embrace, and against the season and the evening that should have brought him home.

331.reading: The wife tells her friend that on the hill where the white blossoms on the low boughs of the black-trunked maraam, its clusters opening, smell so sweet that those crossing the hard waste think of the ones they left, people still call the road her man took a painful one.
331.nuance: The poem sets sweet against painful in adjacent lines (இனிய கமழும், இன்னாது): the scent on the road exists to turn travellers' thoughts homeward, so if even that road is called painful, the pain is his choice to keep going, not the land's.

thinai_evidence.note: a man gone across the hard waste and a wife left behind is the separation of paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (தலைவி இரங்கு பத்து); inferred from the poem: the vocative தோழி and the lament over the man gone across the waste point to the wife speaking to her friend while he is away

332.reading: The wife tells her friend that the herds of beasts of the forest round the high hills are surely without any virtue, since they did not say to him, 'parting from a beloved is cruel; do not go, sir.'
332.nuance: She calls the beasts lawless (அறன் இல) for failing to state a rule of right, that leaving a beloved is cruel: the reproach that belongs to the man is shifted onto the animals he passed. The beasts are the subject of the poem, not a side image, so the deletion test for iraicchi fails.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's parting through the hill forest is the situation

333.reading: The wife asks her friend whether the great flocks of birds in that good stony land are good for nothing at all, since they did not say to him, 'we live joined with our mates; how will you live apart?'
333.nuance: The birds' imagined speech is the argument she could not make: their own paired life is the proof, so she wishes the creatures had used their example where her words failed. As in 332 they are the poem's subject, so this is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the parting across stony country is paalai's situation

334.reading: The wife tells her friend that the man who went through the stony waste where small-leaved nelli grows tall, with her foolish heart following behind him, and who left while her many-petalled kohl-lined eyes wept, is surely harder than stone.
334.nuance: The stone comes back twice: he crosses a land of stones (கல்வாய்) and is harder than stone (கல்லினும் வலியர்), so the country he chose has become his character. Her heart went with him (பின்செல), so what is left behind is only the weeping eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaving through the waste with her heart behind him

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, like a many-petalled flower

335.reading: The wife tells her friend that the roads taken by those who will be long in coming back to them here are said to be very cruel, where the vulture with ears red as blood watches for stinking carrion on the stony slopes.
335.nuance: நீடி இவண் வருநர், 'those who will come here after delay', admits he will return while fixing on the delay; the vulture waiting for flesh is her fear of what the road does to travellers, a mood, not an act of the love situation, so it stays scene and simile.

thinai_evidence.note: fear for the man on the road of the waste

336.reading: The wife tells her friend that those who crossed the waste where summer heat lingers, seized by the sickness for wealth that never stays, surely embraced them as if they would never part.
336.nuance: The wealth he chases is called நின்றது இல், 'what does not stay', the very fault she finds in him: the embrace that seemed to promise permanence and the wealth that cannot keep it are set side by side, and he traded the first for the second.

thinai_evidence.note: the long summer and the waste fix paalai

337.reading: The wife tells her friend that for the man who went to the cold dark hills, wealth is surely sweeter even than the embrace of clasping hands, desired body against body, with her.
337.nuance: She does not say he loves her less; she says he has weighed two sweetnesses and found wealth the sweeter, so the grief is about a measured choice. The last word of the poem is பொருளே, held back to the end like a verdict.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone for wealth is paalai's parting

338.reading: The wife tells her friend that on the slope the tall silk-cotton, blooming leafless, shows at the edge of the waste as a fire on the mountain, and even in this season when parting is hard, their lover is skilled at the hard thing of parting.
338.nuance: The play on அரு is the point: in a season when parting is hard (பிரிவருங் காலை) he is able at what is hard (அரிது வல்லுநர்), so his strength is named in the very word for her pain. The blossom like a hill fire marks the spring that should keep lovers together.

thinai_evidence.note: the leafless silk-cotton in flower at the edge of the waste

comparisons.tenor: the red blossoms of the leafless silk-cotton

339.reading: The wife asks her friend whether, in the land her lover went to, there is no evening, the hour when bats fly up to eat the fragrant fruit of the short-boughed, small-leaved neem.
339.nuance: The question assumes that evening, if it reached him, would bring him home, since it is the hour of longing; she can only explain his staying by supposing his land has no dusk. The bats going to the fruit at evening could be read as creatures returning to what they crave, but they do nothing the lovers do, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening of a wife whose man has gone away

340.reading: The wife asks her friend whether her lover does not think of them, or whether she has fallen into delusion, for he went away and left them while the town's gossip rose like fire in dry bamboo.
340.nuance: Gossip in paalai is unusual: here it does not expose a secret love but mocks a wife who was left, and it spreads with the crackle and speed of a bamboo fire. Her two questions (does he not think of us, or am I deluded) leave open whether the fault is his or hers.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone and left her

links.note: Both have the woman's foolish heart following the man who has left (Ainkurunuru: பேதை நெஞ்சம் பின்செல; Kural: பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு).
links.teaches: With the same words the couplet blames her own heart for going after an unkind man, while the Sangam wife lets the heart go and blames the man as harder than stone, so the following heart was an image that could lay the fault on either lover.

links.note: Akananuru 51's man tells his heart that wealth gained by parting is not worth leaving his wife's embrace; Ainkurunuru 337's wife says that for her man wealth is sweeter than the embrace.
links.teaches: The two poems weigh the same two goods, wealth and the embrace, and reach opposite verdicts according to who speaks: the man at home can still choose the embrace, while the wife whose man has gone can only infer that he chose wealth, so the akam tradition hands each verdict to the one who lives with it.

links.note: Akananuru 1's woman asks whether he has forgotten his word that they would never part (பிரியலம் என்ற சொல்) now that he has gone for gold; Ainkurunuru 336 says he embraced her as if he would never part (பிரியலர் போலப் புணர்ந்தோர்) and went for wealth.
links.teaches: Akananuru 1 rests the betrayal on a spoken vow, while the Ainkurunuru wife rests it on the embrace alone, so together they show that in paalai the embrace itself was read as a promise that the pursuit of wealth broke, with or without words.

links.note: In both the wife, parted from her man, speaks of the evening: the Kural asks the evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru 339 asks whether evening exists in the land he went to.
links.teaches: The couplet gives evening a hard partner of its own, and the Sangam wife supposes his land has no evening at all, so the pair shows the same assumption from two sides: evening is the hour that should force lovers together, and only an absent or hard-hearted partner escapes it.

links.note: In 332 the beasts fail to tell him that parting is cruel; in 333 the birds fail to tell him that they themselves live paired.
links.teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from the argument the beasts should have made by precept (parting is cruel) to the one the birds should have made by their own example (we live with our mates), so the wife tries both ways of restraining a man and puts each in a creature's mouth.

source_issues: 333 line 3: பெர்ந்தோடு is a misprint for பெருந்தோடு (great flock).
334 line 5: அழப்பிர்ந் தோரே is a misprint for அழப்பிரிந் தோரே (who parted, making her weep).
340 line 4: தட்டைத் சென்றனர் நம்மே is a spurious line conflating line 3 (விட்டுச் சென்றனர் நம்மே) with the start of line 5; the poem reads as four lines without it.
